title: Luke 24
description: Luke 24 in the Liberation and Inclusion Translation (LIT).
paragraphs: 1 Before sunrisea on the first day of the week, theyb went to the tomb, carrying the aromatic spices they had prepared. 2 They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,c 3 but upon entering, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus. 4 While they were at a loss about this, suddenly,d two individualse stood beside them in dazzling attire.

5 The womenf were terrified and bowed with their faces to the ground,g but the individualsh said to them, “Why are you looking for the living among the dead? 6 He is not here but has been awakened!i Remember how he told you while he was still in Galilee 7 that it is inevitable for the Son of Humanity to be handed over into the hands of people who deviate, to be crucified, and to be raised up on the third day.”j 8 Then the womenk remembered his words.

9 Returning from the tomb, they brought news of all these things to the Eleven and all the rest. 10 They were Miriaml the Tower,m Joanna,n and Miriam the mother of Jacob,o and the rest of the women who were with them. They started telling the commissioned ones these things, 11 but these words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe them. 12 But getting up, Peter ran to the tomb. Bending down, he saw only the strips of linen, and he went home, wondering to himself what had happened.

13 Significantly,p that same day two of them were traveling to a village called Emmaus, which was about sixty stadiaq from Jerusalem. 14 They were discussing with each other all these things that had happened. 15 While they were discussing and examining them, Jesus himself joined and began traveling with them 16 (their eyes were restrained so as not to recognize him).
17 He said to them, “What are these ideasr you’re tossing back and forth as you’re walking?”
18 In response, one of them, named Cleopas, said to him, “Are you only visiting Jerusalem and don’t know the things that happened there in the last few days?”s
19 “What kinds of things?” he said.

“The things about Jesus of Nazareth,” they told him, “a man who turned out to be a powerful prophet in action and speech, in the view of God and all the people, 20 and how both the lead priests and our leaders handed him over for a sentence of death and crucified him. 21 But we were hoping that he was the one who is coming to purchase liberationt for Israel. And what’s more, in addition to all these things, he is in his third dayu since these things happened. 22 But also, some women from among us shocked us; after having been early at the tomb, 23 and not finding his body, they came claiming also to have seen a vision of messengersv who said he is alive. 24 Some of those with us went to the tomb and found it just as the women said, but they didn’t see him.”

25 Then he said to them, “How obliviousw you are, hesitant in heartx to put your trust in all the things the prophets said! 26 Wasn’t it necessary for the Christy to suffer these things and enter into his praiseworthiness?”z 27 Then, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted the things concerning himself throughout all the scriptures.

28 They got close to the village where they were traveling, and he acted as if he would go further. 29 They pressed him, saying, “Stay with us, because it’s almost evening, and the day is already ending.” And he went in to stay with them.

30 When he had been seated at the tableaa with them, after taking the bread, he spoke praise, and after breaking it, he gave it to them.bb 31 Then their eyes were opened and they recognized him, and he disappeared from their presence.
32 They said to each other, “Weren’t our hearts burning while he was speaking to us on the road, while he was explaining the scriptures to us?”

33 Getting up that very moment, they returned to Jerusalem and found the Eleven and the people who were gathered with them, 34 who were saying, “The Lord really was awakened and was seen by Simeon!”cc 35 Then they recounted the things that happened on the road and how he was recognized by them when he broke the bread.

36 While they were saying these things, Jesusdd himself stood among them and said to them, “May there be well-beingee for you!”ff 37 Panicking, they were terrified, thinking they were seeing a spirit.

38 Then he said to them, “Why are you so shaken? And why do conflicting thoughts arise in your hearts? 39 Look at my hands and my feet: it’s me!gg Touch me and see, since a spirit doesn’t have flesh and bones like you can see that I have.” 40 After saying this, he showed them his hands and feet.

41 While they were still in disbelief (from joy) and wonder, he said to them, “Do you have anything here to eat?” 42 So they gave him a piece of roasted fish, 43 and taking it, he ate it in front of them.

44 Then he said to them, “These are my words I spoke to you while I was still with you, that it is necessary for everything written in Moses’ Torah and the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me to be lived out.”hh 45 Then he openedii their mindsjj for understanding the scriptures, 46 and he told them, “This is the way it is written: for the Christ to suffer and to rise from among the dead on the third day, 47 and for reorientation of the mindkk for the releasell of deviationsmm to be announced in his namenn to all the earth, beginning in Jerusalem. 48 You are witnesses of these things. 49 Look, I am sending my Father’s promise to you, so stay in the city until you’ve been clothed with power from on high.”

50 Then he led them out as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands, he pronounced well-being over them.oo 51 While he was pronouncing well-being over them, he departed from them and was carried up into the heavens.
52 After bowing down to him, they returned to Jerusalem with immense joy 53 and were always in the sacred grounds praising God.

footnotes.label: a
footnotes.html: The Greek idiom used here, orthrou batheos, can mean the period of full darkness right before twilight or the first bit of twilight before the sun appears over the horizon.

footnotes.label: b
footnotes.html: This is referring to the women discussed in Luke 23:55–56.

footnotes.label: c
footnotes.html: Tombs cut into rockface were sealed by rolling a large stone over the opening, sometimes with a channel alongside it to allow opening and closing.

footnotes.label: d
footnotes.html: Literally, “Look!” The word idou is used in a variety of ways, including to draw attention, introduce something surprising or especially noteworthy or mark a turning point.

footnotes.label: e
footnotes.html: Or ‘men.’ The word aner usually refers to adult males, but it is sometimes used to refer to ‘individuals’ of unspecified gender. Tradition holds that the two individuals in this passage are heavenly messengers, which are usually understood not to have a gender, which would also explain why anthropos, which means ‘human,’ isn’t used, though they are sometimes used interchangeably.

footnotes.label: f
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘they’ but ‘the women’ is used for clarity.

footnotes.label: g
footnotes.html: This was a sign of submission, an appeal for mercy from a threatening or powerful figure.

footnotes.label: h
footnotes.html: ‘The individuals’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: i
footnotes.html: The word egeiro has several uses, the most central being ‘get up.’ It is one of the words referring to Jesus being raised from the dead, and it can mean literally standing up or waking up, as well as being presented as a public figure like a prophet. It is often used as the counterpart to the standard euphemism of ‘fall asleep’ used in place of ‘die.’ To resurrect is to ‘wake up’ again.

footnotes.label: j
footnotes.html: Compare with Luke 9:22 and 18:33. Also, notice how this implies that the women were present in those two chapters (or at least in chapter 9) despite not being explicitly named.

footnotes.label: k
footnotes.html: ‘The women’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: l
footnotes.html: ‘Mary’ is the English version of the Greek name Maria, which is itself a transliteration of the Hebrew name Miryam or ‘Miriam,’ which means “beloved” or possibly “bitterness” or “rebellion.” Many names were de-Jewish-ized through layers of translation and tradition, making its original Hebrew roots less visible to modern readers.

footnotes.label: m
footnotes.html: Magdalene means ‘Tower’ in Aramaic.

footnotes.label: n
footnotes.html: ‘Joanna’ is the English version of the Greek name Ioanna, which is itself a transliteration of the Hebrew name Yochanah or Yehochanan, meaning “Yahweh is gracious.” Like many biblical names, it was de-Jewish-ized through layers of translation and tradition, making its original Hebrew roots less visible to modern readers.

footnotes.label: o
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘mother of James.’ This has traditionally been interpreted to be Jesus’ mother.

footnotes.label: p
footnotes.html: Literally, “Look!” The word idou is used in a variety of ways, including to draw attention, introduce something surprising or especially noteworthy or mark a turning point.

footnotes.label: q
footnotes.html: A stadion was approximately 600 feet (or 185 meters) though it varied from region to region. At that estimate, 60 stadia is a little less than seven miles (or a little over eleven kilometers).

footnotes.label: r
footnotes.html: The word logos is traditionally translated ‘word,’ but it has many meanings, including ‘conversation,’ ‘account,’ ‘narrative,’ ‘message,’ ‘saying,’ and more.

footnotes.label: s
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘in these days’

footnotes.label: t
footnotes.html: What is translated here as “purchase liberation” is the word apolutroo in Greek. It is traditionally translated as ‘ransom’ or ‘redeem.’ It literally means securing the release of someone from enslavement by paying the purchase price.

footnotes.label: u
footnotes.html: Most translations render this in such a way that the subject is the time or the day: “it is the third day…” However, the Greek phrase triten tauten hemeran agei fits a common idiom using the verb ago with time to describe passing the time or spending the time in some way. It doesn’t require a description of how or where the time is spent like English typically does, and that idiom is about the person spending the time, not about the amount of time as the subject. Meyer’s Commentary asserts that this verse is being used that way, though others disagree. With Meyer’s perspective, a very literal translation would be “he is spending this third day,” and in English we would supply something like ‘in the tomb’ or ‘dead’ to designate how the day is being spent. The LIT renders it as ‘he is in his third day’ to get close to the idiom without needing to add another word or phrase for it to make sense. The impact of this understanding of it is that this item in the list becomes the most emotionally impactful of the paragraph: it’s the one where the speaker laments that Jesus is dead, not just the events that led to that reality.

footnotes.label: v
footnotes.html: The word angelos means ‘messenger,’ possibly used for spirit beings, but also used for human agents of God (or other people) and sometimes even for natural phenomena. It conveys the meaning of someone authorized to speak—or act—on behalf of another. The reader may faithfully interpret these messengers (acting on God’s behalf) as celestial beings or humans. The word angelos, even for spirit-beings, is a job title, not a ‘species’ classification. The work of Michael S. Heiser is a great source of information on this topic.

footnotes.label: w
footnotes.html: This is technically a word he is using to address them, “Oh, oblivious ones!” but that is unnatural English. The word comes from the root for ‘mind,’ indicating that they are not giving their full minds to it, unable to fully make the connections and understand the significance. It is not a description of their level of long-term intelligence or wisdom.

footnotes.label: x
footnotes.html: The Greek word kardia (usually translated “heart”) describes the deepest core of a person, where thoughts, feelings, desires, motivations, and critical decision-making all come together. It serves as an “inner compass,” giving direction to a person’s life, not just with emotions or for guiding individual decisions, but in shaping the entire way someone sees, trusts, and moves through the world.

footnotes.label: y
footnotes.html: Christos is the Greek translation of the Hebrew mashiach which has traditionally been transliterated as Messiah (and Christ) but translated would literally be “anointed.” The definition of ‘anointed’ is to be ‘smeared with ointment or oil’ and the biblical significance of anointing is to be selected by God (or a prophet of God) for a special appointment, usually king and sometimes other roles like priest or prophet, and experience a ceremony in which the prophet places oil on the head to signify that appointment.

footnotes.label: z
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘glory’

footnotes.label: aa
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘reclined.’ “At the table” is added for clarity. The tables were low to the ground, and people reclined on cushions during meals, not sat in chairs as modern Westerners do.

footnotes.label: bb
footnotes.html: This is the same sequence, using the same words, as what Jesus did during the feeding of the 5,000 in Luke 9:15–16.

footnotes.label: cc
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘Simon.’ Simon is the English transliteration of the Greek transliteration of Simeon. There’s a long history of de-Jewish-ing the names of people in the Bible, including Jesus (Joshua) that stems from pervasive antisemitism.

footnotes.label: dd
footnotes.html: The name ‘Jesus’ is added for clarity.

footnotes.label: ee
footnotes.html: “Well-being” translates the Greek word eirene, which is often rendered “peace.” But like the Hebrew shalom, it implies more than emotional calm. It refers to being restored, healed, whole, reconnected—to God, to community, and to one’s full human dignity.

footnotes.label: ff
footnotes.html: Jesus is doing the exact thing he instructed his students to say to households upon entering in Luke 10:5.

footnotes.label: gg
footnotes.html: Literally, ‘I am he.’

footnotes.label: hh
footnotes.html: Traditionally, ‘fulfilled.’ It could be translated as something like ‘given a fuller meaning.’ It literally means ‘filled full.’ Much like ‘order fulfillment’ when purchasing an order to be delivered, it means to act on something and bring it to reality in a new way.

footnotes.label: ii
footnotes.html: This is the same word for ‘opened’ in the phrase “their eyes were opened” in verse 31.

footnotes.label: jj
footnotes.html: This is the same root for ‘un-minded’ behind what is translated as ‘oblivious’ in verse 25.

footnotes.label: kk
footnotes.html: The Greek word metanoia is traditionally translated as ‘repentance.’ The meaning of metanoia is ‘change the mind’ or ‘transform the mind.’ It does not mean ‘remorse’ or ‘guilt.’ The confusion comes from the Vulgate, the Latin translation of the Bible, which used paenitere, which means ‘to be penitent,’ which was a significant shift away from the Greek meaning. The use of ‘reorient’ here reflects the kind of transformation in view, and it also surfaces the Hebraic understanding of the concept that the biblical writers would have had in mind. The Hebrew word traditionally translated as ‘repent’ was shuv, which literally meant ‘return’ or ‘turn back.’

footnotes.label: ll
footnotes.html: The word here, traditionally translated as “forgiveness,” is never directed toward a person but always directed toward what the person owes. For example, it would not be accurate to phrase it as “forgive us for our debts” but rather “forgive our debts for us.” It’s about sending away, distancing, releasing, letting go, separating from oneself, abandoning or disconnecting from something.

footnotes.label: mm
footnotes.html: The word in Greek here is hamartia, traditionally translated ‘sin.’ The actual meaning is an archery term for missing the target; it’s a metaphor. It evokes an image of veering off course, ending up at an unintended location. It is used regarding many situations, including harmful behavior, disregarding responsibilities as a people or individual called to a specific purpose, and even having chronic illness or debilitating injuries or cultural identities that prohibit one from full participation in temple worship according to the Torah, which is not implied to be wrongdoing but simply not aligned with Torah.

footnotes.label: nn
footnotes.html: Doing something “in the name” of another does not mean to say “in his name” at the end of a prayer. It means to do or say something as a representative of that person, such that your actions are done with the authority and significance that would be given if it were done by that person directly.

footnotes.label: oo
footnotes.html: Or ‘spoke a benediction over them’ or traditionally, ‘blessed them.’ This word eulogeo (related to the English word ‘eulogy’) has to do with speaking over or about someone in a positive way, wishing them well and also attributing worthiness, high esteem to them. It’s both a statement of perceived value and also a proclamation to set positive things in motion for their benefit.
